title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module you should be able to:

title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
text:
Explain the bootstrap principle: treat the sample as a stand-in for the population.
Construct a bootstrap confidence interval for a mean or other statistic.
Interpret a confidence interval correctly.
Use the bootstrap in situations where no formula exists.
Recognize when the bootstrap works and when it doesn’t.

title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
text:
12.1 The Problem
You have a sample of 100 canola fields with a mean yield of 45 bu/ac. What is the mean yield in the population? Well, the sample mean is your best estimate — but it’s not perfect, because of sampling variability (Section 10.3). How much uncertainty is there in the estimate?
The classical answer uses the standard error formula: \(SE = s / \sqrt{n}\), and then a confidence interval of the form \(\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot SE\) (which you will meet formally in AREC 262). But this relies on the sample mean being normally distributed, which relies on the Central Limit Theorem, which requires a “large enough” sample.
What if you want a confidence interval for the median instead of the mean? Or the correlation coefficient? Or the 75th percentile of yields? Or some weird custom statistic? There is no nice formula for the standard error of most of these. The classical approach is stuck.
The bootstrap gets unstuck by doing simulation.

title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
text:
12.2 The Bootstrap Principle
The bootstrap principle is this: your sample is the best information you have about the population, so use it as if it were the population. Repeatedly draw new samples of the same size, with replacement, from your original sample. Each of these “bootstrap samples” is one hypothetical version of what your sample might have been. The spread of the statistic across bootstrap samples is a measure of its sampling variability.
The name comes from the phrase “to pull yourself up by your bootstraps” — doing something that sounds impossible, namely estimating uncertainty from a single sample. But it works.

title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
section: 12.3 Bootstrap Confidence Interval for the Mean
text:
12.3 Bootstrap Confidence Interval for the Mean
Let’s do a concrete example. Suppose you have yields from 50 fields. You want a 95% confidence interval for the mean.
set.seed(42)

# Your sample
yields <- c(48, 52, 47, 55, 50, 41, 46, 49, 53, 45,
            47, 51, 49, 44, 48, 50, 52, 46, 43, 49,
            50, 48, 47, 51, 54, 46, 48, 45, 50, 49,
            47, 52, 48, 50, 46, 49, 47, 51, 48, 50,
            49, 47, 52, 48, 50, 45, 49, 47, 51, 48)

n <- length(yields)
observed_mean <- mean(yields)

# Bootstrap: draw many resamples and compute the mean of each
n_boot <- 10000
boot_means <- replicate(n_boot, mean(sample(yields, n, replace = TRUE)))

# 95% confidence interval: middle 95% of the bootstrap means
ci <- quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))

observed_mean
ci
The two numbers in ci are the lower and upper bounds of the confidence interval. A reasonable interpretation: “we are 95% confident that the population mean lies between the lower and upper bound.”
Actually, let me be careful about interpretation.

title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
section: 12.4 What a Confidence Interval Means (and Does Not)
text:
12.4 What a Confidence Interval Means (and Does Not)
The correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval is:
If we repeated the sampling procedure many times and computed the 95% CI each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true population mean.
This is a statement about the procedure, not about any specific interval. For the interval you have in front of you, either the true mean is in it or it isn’t — we just don’t know which.
In practice, most people read a 95% CI as “I am 95% sure the true mean is in this range,” and that’s close enough for most purposes. But be aware of the subtlety: frequentist CIs are not probability statements about the parameter.
What a confidence interval does tell you:

Point estimate: the center of the interval is your best guess.
Precision: a narrow interval means a precise estimate; a wide interval means “we don’t really know.”
Consistency with hypotheses: if a hypothesized value (say, “the mean is 50”) lies outside the interval, your data is evidence against that hypothesis at the 5% level.

title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
text:
12.5 Bootstrapping Other Statistics
The beauty of the bootstrap is that it works for (almost) any statistic. Just replace mean() with whatever you’re interested in:
# Median
boot_medians <- replicate(10000, median(sample(yields, n, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_medians, c(0.025, 0.975))

# Standard deviation
boot_sds <- replicate(10000, sd(sample(yields, n, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_sds, c(0.025, 0.975))

# 90th percentile
boot_p90 <- replicate(10000, quantile(sample(yields, n, replace = TRUE), 0.9))
quantile(boot_p90, c(0.025, 0.975))
All three of these would be much harder to do with closed-form formulas. The bootstrap makes them trivial.

title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
text:
12.6 Bootstrapping a Regression Coefficient
Here’s a more sophisticated example. You fit a linear regression of yield on fertilizer and want a confidence interval for the slope. The classical CI uses a formula based on normal-distribution assumptions. The bootstrap CI makes no such assumption.
# Suppose you have a data frame `yields` with columns yield and fertilizer
observed_slope <- coef(lm(yield ~ fertilizer, data = yields))["fertilizer"]

boot_slopes <- replicate(10000, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(yields), nrow(yields), replace = TRUE)
  boot_sample <- yields[idx, ]
  coef(lm(yield ~ fertilizer, data = boot_sample))["fertilizer"]
})

quantile(boot_slopes, c(0.025, 0.975))
This is a fully honest confidence interval for the slope of the regression, without assuming normality. For a large enough sample, the two CIs (classical and bootstrap) will be very similar. For small samples or non-normal data, the bootstrap can be meaningfully different — and more honest.

title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
section: 12.7 When the Bootstrap Works and When It Doesn’t
text:
12.7 When the Bootstrap Works and When It Doesn’t
The bootstrap is remarkable but not magic. A few things to know:

Small samples. With \(n < 20\) or so, the bootstrap gets wobbly. You are resampling from a tiny set, and there are not enough different possibilities. For very small samples, classical methods (or more sophisticated bootstraps) can work better.
Extremes. The bootstrap is not great for estimating the maximum, the minimum, or other extreme quantiles. By definition, the resample contains at most what the original sample contained — so the maximum never increases.
Dependent data. If your observations are correlated (time series, spatial data, repeated measures from the same farm), the simple bootstrap underestimates uncertainty. Fancier “block bootstraps” exist for these cases.
Biased statistics. If your statistic has bias, the bootstrap estimates its distribution but doesn’t remove the bias.

For most of what you will do in AREC 261, the bootstrap is a safe and sensible default.

title: 12  Bootstrap Methods
text:
12.8 Bootstrap vs Permutation
A confusing point: both bootstrap and permutation tests involve resampling. What’s the difference?

Permutation tests are for hypothesis testing. They answer “is there a difference?” by shuffling labels to see what would happen if there weren’t.
Bootstrap is for confidence intervals and uncertainty quantification. It answers “how precise is my estimate?” by resampling with replacement to see how the estimate varies.

They look similar in code but answer different questions. Use permutation when you are testing a null hypothesis; use bootstrap when you want a confidence interval or standard error.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
How to use this page
These ten practice questions use two synthetic datasets. Download them, open them in Excel, and answer each question by building the appropriate formula, PivotTable, or chart. Each question has a collapsible Answer section — try the question yourself before peeking.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Datasets

canola_yields_2025.csv — 50 canola fields in Saskatchewan in 2025, with columns field_id, region, variety, acres, yield_bu_ac, fertilizer_kg_ha, irrigated.
farm_costs_2025.csv — 40 input-cost orders for a grain farm in 2025, with columns order_id, order_date, supplier, product, price_per_unit, quantity, unit.

A short tip before you start: import CSVs using Data → Get Data → From Text/CSV rather than double-clicking, so Excel does not mangle any of the values.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Question 1 — Mean yield
Compute the mean yield (in bu/ac) across all 50 fields in canola_yields_2025.csv. Place the result in a labelled cell and round to two decimal places for display.


Answer


Expected value: 44.35 bu/ac
Formula: =AVERAGE(E2:E51) (assuming yield is in column E, rows 2-51)
Why: The mean is the sum of the values divided by the count. AVERAGE does this in one call. If your answer is off by even 0.01 bu/ac, check whether you included the header row or missed the last row.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Question 2 — Median yield
Compute the median yield (in bu/ac) for the same dataset.


Answer


Expected value: 45.40 bu/ac
Formula: =MEDIAN(E2:E51)
Why it matters: The median is the middle value when the data is sorted. Because it is resistant to outliers, it is often a better “typical” value than the mean, especially for skewed data. Here the median (45.4) is slightly higher than the mean (44.35), suggesting a mild left skew — a few low-yielding fields pulling the mean down.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Question 3 — Standard deviation of yield
Compute the sample standard deviation of yield across all 50 fields.


Answer


Expected value: 5.16 bu/ac
Formula: =STDEV.S(E2:E51)
Why STDEV.S and not STDEV.P? STDEV.S uses \(n-1\) in the denominator (Bessel’s correction) and is the right choice when your 50 fields are a sample from a larger population. STDEV.P divides by \(n\) and is only right when you literally have the entire population in front of you. For virtually all data analysis work, use STDEV.S.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Question 4 — 90th percentile of yield
Compute the 90th percentile of yield (the yield that 90% of fields fall below).


Answer


Expected value: 51.06 bu/ac
Formula: =PERCENTILE.INC(E2:E51, 0.9)
Interpretation: A field with a yield of 51.06 bu/ac is in the top 10% of this dataset. Percentiles are how crop insurance, government support programs, and variety trials describe performance — get comfortable with them. If you got a slightly different number with PERCENTILE.EXC, that’s fine — the two versions use different interpolation methods. For this course, use .INC.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Question 5 — Count of above-average fields
How many fields have a yield strictly greater than 48 bu/ac?


Answer


Expected value: 12 fields
Formula: =COUNTIF(E2:E51, ">48")
Watch out for: The criterion must be a text string in quotes when using comparison operators: ">48", not >48. This trips up almost every beginner at least once. Also note that COUNTIF with ">48" is strict — a yield of exactly 48 is not counted. If you want at-or-above, use ">=48".

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Question 6 — Regional average
Compute the average yield of fields in the “South” region only.


Answer


Expected value: 42.41 bu/ac
Formula: =AVERAGEIF(B2:B51, "South", E2:E51)
Alternative: You could also build a PivotTable with region on Rows and yield_bu_ac as Values (set to Average). A PivotTable is more flexible if you want to see all three regional averages at once — question 7 is a good place to try that.
Sanity check: The South average (42.4) is lower than the overall mean (44.4), which is consistent with the hint in the dataset generator (southern fields have a slightly lower baseline yield).

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
section: Question 7 — Variety with most total acres
text:
Question 7 — Variety with most total acres
Which variety has the largest total acres planted across all 50 fields?


Answer


Expected value: DKTC 9105, with 3,090 total acres
How to find it: The cleanest approach is a PivotTable:

Click anywhere in the data and choose Insert → PivotTable.
Put variety on Rows and acres in Values (set to Sum).
Sort the table by total acres descending.

Alternative (formula-only): =SUMIF(C2:C51, "DKTC 9105", D2:D51) will give you the total for one specific variety, but you would need to run it four times and compare. PivotTables are purpose-built for this kind of “grouped summary” question — it is worth learning them now.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Question 8 — Total production
Compute the total production (in bushels) across all 50 fields. Note that production = yield (bu/ac) × acres.


Answer


Expected value: 476,208.4 bushels (approximately)
Formula: =SUMPRODUCT(D2:D51, E2:E51)
Why SUMPRODUCT? It multiplies two ranges element-wise and then sums the results, all in one step. The long way would be: add a helper column F with =D2*E2 copied down, then =SUM(F2:F51). Both work, but SUMPRODUCT is cleaner and a useful tool to have in your back pocket.
Unit check: acres × (bu/ac) = bushels. Always stop and check that units cancel properly before trusting a computed total.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Question 9 — Spending with one supplier
In farm_costs_2025.csv, compute the total amount spent with “Prairie Ag Supply” across all orders (price per unit × quantity, summed across all their orders).


Answer


Expected value: $6,221.00
Formula: =SUMPRODUCT((C2:C41="Prairie Ag Supply")*E2:E41*F2:F41)
How it works: (C2:C41="Prairie Ag Supply") returns an array of TRUE/FALSE values. Multiplying converts them to 1/0, which zeros out any row that is not Prairie Ag Supply. Then SUMPRODUCT multiplies price × quantity × (1 or 0) and sums the result.
Alternative: Add a helper column =E2*F2 (line total), then =SUMIF(C2:C41, "Prairie Ag Supply", G2:G41). Both are valid — the helper-column version is more readable for beginners, and the SUMPRODUCT version is more compact.

title: Module 1 — Test Bank
text:
Question 10 — Highest Urea price
Across all orders in farm_costs_2025.csv, what is the highest price per unit ever paid for Urea?


Answer


Expected value: $0.95 per kg
Formula: =MAXIFS(E2:E41, D2:D41, "Urea")
Alternative (older Excel): {=MAX(IF(D2:D41="Urea", E2:E41))} entered as an array formula with Ctrl+Shift+Enter. MAXIFS is much cleaner and works from Excel 2019 onwards.
Practical note: A single random draw with a fixed seed means there may only be a handful of Urea orders in this dataset. In a real analysis, always check the count of matching rows (COUNTIF(D2:D41, "Urea")) before trusting a max — a max computed from three observations is not very meaningful.
